title: SIM-GRAPH: A universal guide to symmetric interactions
authors: R. C. Verstraten, C. Morais Smith
abstract: Symmetry plays a central role throughout physics, from Fourier analysis on discrete lattices to the classification of elementary particles in the standard model. In finite quantum systems, symmetries are often discrete, such as reflection and rotational symmetries. Here, we present the SIM-GRAPH method (Symmetric Ising Models - Graph Reduction And Projected Hamiltonians), which uses such symmetries to efficiently calculate ground-state observables of interacting quantum systems. By projecting all interactions onto a symmetric subset of the system, the method effectively reduces the number of sites, thus providing an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization. Furthermore, we introduce two extensions that broaden the applicability of the method and allow for a controlled trade-off between computational cost and accuracy.
summary: This paper introduces SIM-GRAPH, a novel computational method that leverages underlying symmetries in quantum Hamiltonians to drastically reduce the effective size of the system being simulated. By projecting interactions onto a symmetric subspace, it achieves an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization for calculating ground-state properties. It is highly valuable for studying large, interacting quantum spin systems like the TFIM on various complex lattices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is efficiently calculating ground-state observables of interacting quantum many-body systems, which typically suffer from exponentially scaling Hilbert space dimensions.
main_result: The SIM-GRAPH method provides an exponential speedup over standard exact diagonalization by projecting interactions onto a symmetry-reduced graph, achieving high accuracy on various lattices.
method: The method, SIM-GRAPH, maps the Hamiltonian onto a graph, uses group theory to identify symmetries, and constructs a symmetry-reduced Hamiltonian by projecting interactions onto the symmetric subset of sites.
model_or_system: The method is applied to interacting quantum many-body systems, specifically modeling the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM) on various lattices (1D chains, 2D square lattices, Sierpinski triangles).
key_observables: Ground-state observables, notably the average ground-state magnetization ($\langle n_\uparrow angle$).
important_parameters: The ratio of transverse field ($\Omega$) to coupling strength ($\Delta$), and the size/geometry of the lattice (e.g., 3x3, 4x4).
main_assumptions: The method is projective, meaning computed eigenenergies are guaranteed to be greater than or equal to the true eigenenergies, and it assumes that the ground state can be accurately represented by the symmetric subspace.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graph reduction process for lattices (e.g., 3x3), compare ground-state magnetization vs. field ratio for different lattices (1D and 2D), and show convergence studies using various SIM2.n methods.
paper_structure: The paper introduces SIM-GRAPH, details its application to the TFIM on various geometries (1D, 2D, Sierpinski), and systematically compares its results against Exact Diagonalization (ED) using increasingly refined projection techniques (SIM2.n and SIM3).
why_interesting: The technique of exploiting underlying symmetries to reduce the effective dimensionality of the Hilbert space is highly relevant for simulating complex quantum materials where symmetries are known or suspected.

The three dis- tinct symmetric representations Si are highlighted in red on the left hand side. On the right hand side, we see the reduced graph, where all interactions are projected to the symmetric subset and the other sites are removed. The remaining sites are relabeled to a counting order.

FIG. 2. The average ground-state magnetization of the TFIM on the 3 × 3 square lattice is presented at V/Ω= 10 for both NN and VdW interactions, computed using both ED and SIM-GRAPH. For better visual comparison, the exact results are plotted using larger points, with the SIM-GRAPH results overlaid in points half the size. For both NN and VdW interactions, we find excellent agreement with only minor de- viations from the exact results.

FIG. 3. The average ground-state magnetization of the TFIM on the 4 × 4 square lattice is presented at V/Ω= 10 for both NN and VdW interactions, computed on 50 points using both ED and SIM-GRAPH. For both NN and VdW interactions, we find deviations up to 4 spins away from the exact results. Besides the high and low ∆/Ωlimits, we find only one region of agreement at ⟨n↑⟩= 8, which corresponds to the checker- board states.
